Gemini Agent is built for high-ceiling work where EACH task gets its own computer.  

You can choose Gemini 4 Argon or Claude Opus 5.5. 

10 things that make it a universal work Agent (read till the end to see what a REAL work agent looks like): 

1. One Agent, one API
Chat, autonomous objectives, and code generation from a single interface. Assign it work, schedule it, or have it respond to events.

2. Coworker agents with their own identities
It creates job-specific sub-agents, each with its own identity, and computer running in parallel for hours or days.

Each Coworker agent gets its own Workspace account: an agent email, calendar, Drive, and presence in your company directory. You mention it in Chat. It acts under its own identity, not yours, and sees only what you share.

3. Everywhere, including headless
Web, iOS, Android, Windows, Mac, command line, Workspace, Microsoft 365, Slack. It also runs as a headless agent with no dedicated interface.

4. Work 24/7 in the cloud
It keeps one set of memories, context, and personalization graph across every device and channel. Work that takes hours or days keeps running after you close your laptop. You never have to re-brief it.

5. Layers of memory that improve over time
- Session: the task in front of it, even when it runs for days.
- Semantic: a structured knowledge base it builds as it reads documents, talks to people, and works with other agents.
- Procedural: how a job gets done, including skills it writes for itself.
- Episodic: everything it has done before.

6. Proactive by design
It does not wait to be prompted. An email asking you for a deck gets flagged as delegatable, one click to hand off. Your inbox ranks by what matters, not by what just arrived, and tells you why.

7. Tools and skills, with company registries
Salesforce, ServiceNow, Jira, Git, Confluence, Microsoft 365, Slack, BigQuery, Databricks, Postgres, Snowflake, your desktop files, and any MCP server inside or outside your network. Teams publish their own tools and skills to a shared company registry.

8. Model Choice so you are not locked in
It runs each job on the model that fits best, running  across the Gemini and Claude models from Anthropic today, with other private and open models to come. 

9. Governed like an employee
Every agent gets a cryptographically attested identity with least-privilege permissions, and an audit trail attributed to the agent rather than a person. Agents run in a sandbox behind Agent Gateway, an AI network firewall. Write the policy once and it applies to every agent.

10. Costs you can actually cap
Smart Routing puts each workload on the model with the best performance at the lowest cost. Set a hard spend limit in Cloud Billing and that project's agent pauses until you resume it in one click.

parent_text:
When LLM demand exceeds capacity, which requests should go first?

Model providers already offer a few priority tiers. But even within a tier, requests compete for compute, and users value latency differently. Your coding agent might be blocked due to a request that belongs to an unattended background job.

Why not let the market decide?

In our new paper, Inference Auctions, users bid for request priority, and our auction allocates that priority to those who value it most.

Unfortunately, naively selling to the highest bidders destroys prefix-cache locality, increasing SGLang's average latency by up to 12x in our experiments.

Our fix is to run an auction over depth-first search traversals of the request prefix tree, ordering subtrees by average bid. This maximizes social welfare while retaining cache optimality, with VCG payments incentivizing truthful bidding, and the resulting request order preserves key performance metrics (cache hits and mean TTFT) of the underlying scheduler. 

w/ @keegan_w_harris @sidpra5ad @nhaghtal and Michael Jordan

parent_text:
Apple and CMU Make Small Agents Reason Faster by Choosing, Not Generating
A search agent may spend hundreds of tokens explaining its next move, even when the decision is simply “search for a fact” or “inspect the image.”
Apple and CMU's Selection-based Structured Reasoning (SSR) replaces that repeated generation with strategy selection. Their experiments cut per-turn reasoning latency by over 90%, while preserving comparable task success.
Zhihu contributor ZixuuuFive, a researcher on the team, shares how it works.

Different questions often need the same strategy
The team found that multimodal search trajectories repeatedly use a small set of high-level decisions.
Identifying an exhibition inside a pictured building and finding a company's founding year involve different facts. But once the entity is known, both can follow the same strategy: search using the entity's name and the missing attribute.
SSR turns these recurring decisions into six reusable natural-language options:
Identify an unknown entity through image search, look up a fact through text search, or crop and inspect image details.
Answer from collected evidence, answer directly from the image, or answer using existing knowledge.

The same library is shared across all tested benchmarks. After selecting a strategy, the model still freely generates the query, tool arguments, crop coordinates, or final answer.
The language model is also the selector
SSR scores each candidate's full text using its length-normalized log-likelihood under the current context. A softmax converts those scores into a probability distribution, from which the strategy is sampled.
Selection and action generation share the same model parameters and system prompt. No separate classification head is required.
This is not just predicting a strategy ID. In an ablation, replacing full-text scoring with candidate-number selection reduced success, suggesting the options' semantic content matters.

Known candidates make parallel scoring possible
Free-form thinking requires sequential, token-by-token decoding. SSR already knows every candidate's text.
With teacher forcing, it evaluates candidate-token likelihoods in a batched forward pass. Candidates are scored simultaneously while sharing the context KV cache.
The strategy-selection stage therefore generates no new tokens autoregressively. Action generation still does.
In one illustrative example, free-form reasoning took 1,821 ms and chose the wrong action. SSR selected the appropriate strategy in 32 ms.

Training covers both selection and execution
For SFT, SSR jointly optimizes a cross-entropy loss over strategy choices and a generation loss over action tokens.
For RL methods such as GRPO, GSPO, and SAPO, the reasoning-token importance ratio is replaced with a categorical ratio for the selected strategy, alongside the standard clipped objective.
Because selection is restricted to the library by construction, SSR can train directly with RL, without an SFT warm start to teach the reasoning format.

The speedup has a specific scope
The team evaluated Qwen3-VL 2B/4B across seven multimodal search benchmarks, using H100 GPUs and SGLang offline inference.
The 4B SSR model trained with GRPO achieved 61.37% average success, comparable to the cited same-size TAPO+GSPO baseline's 61.25%.
Per-turn reasoning latency fell by over 90%. Total model inference latency per question fell by 28-54%, not 90%.
Across four training objectives, SSR maintained success rates comparable to the corresponding free-form reasoning models.

A smaller reasoning space, not an agent that stops thinking
Increasing the library from one generic option to six raised average success from 37.24% to 61.37%. Selection also adapted to the task: image-based answering dominated one benchmark, while image inspection was more common on high-resolution questions.
The broader argument is that strategy-level reasoning need not always be unrestricted language generation.
Open-ended proofs and code design still benefit from expressive reasoning. But recurring search and tool-use decisions can operate within a compact, meaningful strategy space, while leaving task-specific execution open-ended.

parent_text:
Qwen3.8-27B at 200+ tok/s per user on an Apple M5 Max.

LithosAI is open-sourcing lithos-metal, an inference engine built around Metal megakernels and DSpark speculative decoding.

The goal is simple: make local inference fast enough that running a coding agent on your Mac feels much closer to working with a fast hosted model.

But the interesting part is how they’re doing it.

1. Megakernels reduce the overhead between operations

Traditional inference engines often execute a model through many separate GPU kernel launches. Each operation produces intermediate data that the next operation must consume, sometimes requiring additional memory writes, reads and synchronization.

Lithos-metal takes a different approach.

It generates specialized Metal megakernels that combine multiple operations into a larger GPU program. Instead of repeatedly dispatching small kernels, it can coordinate related computations within a single dispatch.

That creates opportunities to reuse intermediate values in registers or on-chip memory, reduce unnecessary data movement and schedule independent work more efficiently.

The compiler also manages dependencies between operations, so fusion doesn’t mean blindly cramming the entire model into one enormous kernel.

For Qwen3.8-27B, LithosAI focuses on the model’s Gated DeltaNet and full-attention layers, while keeping other operations separate where that makes more sense.

2. DSpark helps the model generate multiple tokens per verification pass

The second component is DSpark speculative decoding.

Instead of asking the main model to generate every token sequentially, a smaller draft model proposes a block of tokens. The main model then verifies those proposals together and commits the accepted sequence.

When several proposals are accepted, one target-model pass can produce multiple output tokens.

The challenge is keeping the draft model cheap enough that drafting and verification cost less than ordinary decoding.

Lithos-metal combines DSpark with its optimized GPU execution path to reduce that overhead.

3. Why this matters on Apple Silicon

LLM decoding often spends much of its time moving model weights and intermediate data rather than performing arithmetic alone.

That makes memory bandwidth, data reuse and kernel scheduling especially important.

Apple Silicon gives developers a different environment from a discrete NVIDIA GPU. Lithos-metal is designed around Metal and the specific capabilities of Apple’s GPUs, including accelerated matrix operations and flexible on-chip memory.

The result is a runtime tailored to the hardware rather than a generic inference engine simply running on a Mac.

4. What about the performance?

LithosAI reports peak throughput above 200 tokens per second per user for Qwen3.8-27B on an M5 Max.

That figure needs context. Peak throughput isn’t automatically the sustained speed of every prompt or coding session. The blog’s performance analysis shows that context length affects results, with its projected target-compute throughput reaching roughly 127 tok/s at 32K context.

Still, the direction is interesting: the team is attacking both sides of decoding, reducing execution overhead with megakernels and amortizing target-model work with speculative decoding.

The project is open source, so developers can inspect the implementation, reproduce measurements and test their own workloads.

You can also try it with a coding agent through the project’s one-command workflow.

The bigger takeaway is that local inference speed isn’t determined by model size alone.

The model matters. So do the kernels, memory traffic, scheduling and speculative decoding strategy around it.

A 27B model is one thing. Making it fast enough to keep a coding agent responsive on a laptop is an entirely different engineering problem. https://t.co/jq94neshAU

parent_text:
Your agent made the API 10x faster. Unfortunately, it stopped doing half the work.

Imagine an endpoint that returns 100 orders with customer names. The agent reports roughly 1,000 ms down to 100 ms. Tests pass.

Maybe it replaced 100 separate customer lookups with one batched query. That could explain a genuine 10x gain.

Or it removed the lookups entirely. No customer names, but the benchmark only checks HTTP 200 and the order count.

To be fair, the wrong response does arrive much faster.

“Optimized data fetching” would look equally at home in either PR summary. Ask where the 900 ms went.

For the batching change, the agent should be able to show that repeated database calls ate most of the original time, those calls disappeared, and the full response still contains the correct customer data under the same workload.

If the traces show those calls only took 20 ms, the other 880 ms have apparently been left as an exercise for the reviewer.

That question also helps when the optimization is good. Once the agent accounts for the remaining 100 ms, you know where further work might pay off. If 80 ms is now spent fetching orders, there’s a limit to how much faster you can make this by rearranging the customer lookup code again.

Put the explanation in the original task: account for the time saved, verify the same work and results, and show what’s slow now. Bring measurements.

It saves a lot of follow-up questions, starting with “where are the names?”

Build your own harness, folks.

Reading papers like this makes me realize how underexplored harness engineering really is.

The authors find that on whole-repository migration, GPT-5.6 Sol goes from 6.5% to 31.0% when Codex is replaced with the HERMES harness, with the same model and effort setting.

marin update: spent the last few days trying to squeeze more speed out of my rust + cuda inference engine and the results are kinda crazy lol

here's what changed:

8k token prompts went from 25.4s ->  5.9s before the first word appears. turns out my attention code wasn't even using the gpu's tensor cores properly. rewrote it and got ~4.3x faster prefill while using 77% less gpu energy.

long convos no longer slow down generation nearly as much. found that the gpu was reading the kv cache in tiny chunks. fixed those reads and went from 18 -> 35 tokens/sec at 16k context. almost 2x faster.

marin can now remember convos across restarts. instead of processing thousands of old tokens again, it saves the kv cache to disk and restores it. resuming a ~4k token conversation went from ~6.5s -> 0.22s to first token.

kv cache now uses half the memory with fp16 without noticeably changing the answers in my tests.

int8 weights are working in normal chat too. ~1.7gb less vram and up to 63% faster generation. still optional since i'm not fully happy with the quality tradeoffs yet.

also tried a bunch of things that didnt work including using a smaller model to guess the next tokens. (will try this later on after some more minor optimizations) 

honestly the funniest part is how many bottlenecks turned out to be my own cuda kernels.

Takeaways from my fireside chat with the lead of the Marin project, David Hall @dlwh, at the Frontier Data Summit yesterday:

Topic: "How benchmarks are (and aren't) used in model development today"

Takeaways:
- Benchmarks typically occupy one square of a 2x2 grid: pretraining vs posttraining, and internal development vs external communication; posttraining x external ("model card evals") are the household names, but not the only benchmarks that matter
- The best evals for internal development work at multiple scales, so they can guide scaling laws and give signal weeks or months before the model scores something non-zero on traditional model card benchmarks
- Pretraining tends to mostly rely on metrics derived from the pretraining corpus like loss/perplexity, since most benchmarks being built today are built for post-trained models where models may score 0 for months during training; some older evals with short answer types (e.g. multiple choice) also work (e.g. MMLU)
- Evals that isolate a particular property are particularly helpful for guiding decisions during development -- e.g. GraphWalks,  MRCR, etc. Doing well on them is necessary but not sufficient to develop a great model. Note that both of these are synthetic; there's a place for those
- Evals we wish existed: more like Terminal Bench Lite (h/t OpenThoughts, @terminalbench, @SnorkelAI, @bespokelabsai) -- intentionally simpler variants of frontier tasks that correlate well with the model card versions but provide signal for smaller models and in earlier stages of development

If you've got an idea for a killer benchmark, get it funded and supported with an Open Benchmarks Grant: https://t.co/ilT5J5k914

The HIGAgentSkills repo distills Apple's Human Interface Guidelines into instructions an agent can follow, and Peter Friese's pitch for it was blunt: no coding agent has good taste for UI unless you teach it with a skill. He's onto a narrow fix for a much bigger problem.

Models default to purple-to-blue gradient heroes, Inter as the only font anyone's agent seems to know, card-in-card layouts, and rounded icon tiles stacked above every heading, because a model trained on the whole internet converges on the statistical average of design, and the average is bland by definition. This is the same wall web design hit around 2015, when half the internet ran the same Bootstrap template with a different logo pasted on top, until design systems from Stripe, Linear, and a handful of others gave people something specific to copy instead of the default.

The fix now takes the same shape, just packaged as a Skill instead of a framework. Anthropic ships frontend-design as a baseline that bans the overused fonts outright. Impeccable runs 59 deterministic detection rules through a CLI that can gate a CI build on contrast and spacing violations. Emil Kowalski's motion skill hands agents real easing curves and a 44 pixel minimum hit area instead of a guess. Introducing the Arena Alignment Index, our new benchmark measuring safety and alignment of AI agents in real-world use.

Built from 90K+ real-world agent sessions across 27 models, the index measures three critical signals:
- Unauthorized Action (UA): Taking actions beyond the user's instructions or permissions
- False Attribution (FA): Attributing statements or actions that are contradicted by user-provided evidence
- Deceptive Completion (DC): Claiming a task was completed when it was not.

Key findings:
- OpenAI models currently lead the Alignment Index
- Rogue actions are rare, but can have serious consequences when they occur
- Agents can mislead users about task progress
- Misalignment risks increase with conversation length
- Safety and alignment are improving across model generations

As agents take on longer, more complex, and higher-stakes tasks, measuring not just what they can accomplish, but how safely and reliably they act, becomes increasingly important.

Qwen3.8-27B running at nearly 70 tok/s with a 262K context window on a 12GB GPU sounds impossible until you look at the engineering behind it.

The setup uses Mirai S Qwen3.8-27B, a heavily compressed 2.4-bit model weighing roughly 11GB, converted to GGUF for a custom llama.cpp fork without re-quantizing the original weights.

The initial port ran on an RTX 3090 limited to 12GB VRAM and managed about 38 tok/s with an 82K context.

Then CaryPalmerr optimized the runtime.

Same GPU. Same model file. Very different results:

• 262,144-token context
• ~69.9 tok/s decode
• ~1,124 tok/s prefill
• 11.7GB peak VRAM
• Q8 KV cache

The key is how the runtime handles memory.

Instead of forcing the entire KV cache into VRAM, it splits the cache between GPU memory and pinned system RAM. MTP speculative decoding helps improve generation speed without requiring a larger GPU.

That combination makes 12GB VRAM a constraint to engineer around rather than an absolute ceiling.

The model officially supports 262K context, but making that practical on a single 12GB card is a separate challenge from simply supporting it on paper.

There’s another experiment built around the same compressed weights.

Because the trellis-coded model can’t be modified like a conventional checkpoint, the project measures the refusal direction on the quantized model and applies the transformation during inference.

Reported results:
• 64/64 harmful prompts refused → 0/64
• 78/82 held-out prompts refused → 0/82
• Decode speed: 69.9 → 69.7 tok/s

Those numbers need context. The refusal counts were measured using regex, and one of 24 tests still refused with thinking enabled. Long-context speed also drops, reaching around 27.9 tok/s at roughly 60K context in the reported RTX 3090 setup.

So the real story isn’t simply a compressed model running fast.

It’s the combination of 2.4-bit weights, split KV-cache memory, pinned RAM and speculative decoding making a large model usable on hardware with limited VRAM.

The lesson for local AI is becoming clearer: the weights alone don’t determine what your hardware can run.

Memory movement, caching and the inference runtime matter just as much.

The model is only half the system. https://t.co/dImOPy5VgT

Seven days ago, we started an experiment in Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI).

We wanted to explore a simple question: What happens when we let an AI agent iteratively improve its own harness?

So we let Lobe Agent run for an entire week, using our RSI framework to explore and optimize its own harness.

Today, we're sharing the results.

We evaluated the resulting system on FrontierHarness, using Kimi K3 as the underlying model.

Key results:

• 70.0% pass rate (21/30), ranking #1 among 13 harnesses in our preliminary comparison.

• $1.68 per successful task, compared to $3.47 for Codex and $18.34 for Claude Code.

• 86.2% median cache hit rate, with a median completion time of 7m 19s on successful tasks.

These preliminary results suggest that harness-level optimization may be a promising path toward improving agent performance and efficiency without modifying the underlying model weights.

The comparison includes selected retries and differences in execution environments, and should not be interpreted as an official leaderboard ranking.

We plan to fully open-source the experiment's scripts, execution trajectories, and a detailed technical report to enable reproducibility and further investigation.

Alongside this experiment, we've also been building Awesome-RSI, an open-source research map of Recursive Self-Improvement.

The repository brings together papers, frameworks, benchmarks, and open-source projects spanning model-level and harness-level self-improvement, automated AI research, and safety.

We may be overestimating how much a complex harness adds to a model’s capabilities.

If a workflow was added because an older model couldn’t handle something, we should reconsider it when a stronger model takes over.

If the model can already break down tasks, choose tools, and check its own work, how much of our scaffolding is still necessary? Could it keep adding calls and context without improving results?

What Does a Harness Buy? Tokens, mostly, got me thinking about this.

The authors held the model fixed and compared Claude Code, mini-SWE-agent, and OpenCode. Across 447 tasks and two Qwen models, Claude Code and the largely bash-based mini-SWE-agent were equivalent within a predefined margin of ±5 percentage points. The fuller framework showed no clear advantage in solving these tasks.

Costs differed much more clearly: with the same model and consistent pricing, the most expensive harness cost roughly three times as much per task as the cheapest. System prompts, tool definitions, and the number of calls all affected the bill. 

Some harness complexity may persist because our assumptions haven’t caught up with the model.

An earlier model made mistakes, so we added a check. It struggled with a task, so we prescribed a workflow. Several model generations later, those designs remain, and every run keeps paying for them.
That’s a hypothesis, though. The paper doesn’t establish that stronger models necessarily need simpler harnesses.

But it suggests a useful experiment: with every model upgrade, try removing steps previously considered essential. See which tasks actually suffer. Keep recovery and context management where they help; let designs that no longer improve results disappear.

We’re used to describing a framework’s progress through what it adds.
Progress in the model should also show up in how much we can finally remove from the harness.

You can now train your own decision model in our platform AC2! Jev-like models, custom fit for your use case :)

We implement decision models through a language-model backbone with a small learned output layer called a decision head. The backbone processes the input, question, and answer choices, and the head produces scores which are softmaxed to produce a probability distribution over answer choices.

Our software interface makes it easy to add a variable-sized decision head to frontier open-weight models. Choose any open source model, and train it as a decision model using Brier loss or cross-entropy loss. Training updates both the decision head and the language backbone.

We tried it on 50k sampled training datapoints from the Civil Comments dataset, starting from Perplexity’s pplx-decider-v1-27b, and F1 for detecting toxic comments increased from 0.482 to 0.677 on 20k sampled eval datapoints. The training job took less than an hour on four B300 GPUs.

Agent evaluations are hard to reproduce. This framework gives you a concrete environment.

AgentEnv Framework is a Python SDK and CLI for builders creating agentic environments and tasks that grade agents inside them.

It helps you move from an environment definition to a repeatable agent run by building containerized environments into versioned images, deploying them behind a gateway, and scoring what the agent did.

Key features:

• Environment protocol – containerized servers speak the open agentenv-framework-protocol
• Agent task grading – point an agent at an environment and score what it did
• Versioned images – build environments into versioned images before deployment
• Fast local starting point – run the built-in hello task with no Docker, model, or configuration
• Plugin extension points – installed packages can register environments, task steps, artifacts, providers, and explorer plugins

It’s open-source (Apache License 2.0 license).

parent_text:
Day 135 — Becoming AI Engineer

Today I learned an important engineering lesson while building DocMind:

Retrieval isn't just about finding relevant chunks. It's about making a sequence of ranking decisions under a latency budget.

Yesterday, I built the indexing layer with two searchable representations:

→ Vector index for semantic retrieval
→ BM25 index for lexical retrieval
Today, I connected them into a single retrieval pipeline.

The goal was to understand how each stage contributes to retrieval quality and what it costs.

I started with hybrid retrieval.

Vector search helps find conceptually related content, even when the query uses different wording from the source.

BM25 helps identify exact terminology, product names, error messages, and technical identifiers.

Neither method is sufficient for every query.

So I wanted to combine their strengths rather than assume one retrieval method would handle everything.

But combining them introduced another problem.

Vector similarity scores and BM25 scores aren't directly comparable.

A higher score from one method doesn't necessarily mean the result is more relevant than a result from the other.

I used Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) to merge the two ranked lists.

Instead of comparing raw scores, RRF uses the position of each chunk in its respective ranking.

This allows chunks that perform well across both retrieval methods to receive a stronger combined ranking.

The pipeline now looks like this:

Query → Vector Search + BM25 → RRF → Cross-Encoder Reranking → Relevance Check

The next decision was reranking.

Initial retrieval needs to be relatively inexpensive because it must search broadly enough to avoid missing useful evidence.

A cross-encoder can evaluate relevance more directly by processing the query and candidate chunk together, but doing this for every chunk would increase latency and computational cost.

So I added a two-stage approach:

→ Retrieve candidates using vector search and BM25
→ Merge rankings using RRF
→ Rerank only the top-N candidates with a cross-encoder

This introduced another engineering trade-off.
If N is too small, relevant chunks may never reach the reranker.
If N is too large, the system spends more time reranking candidates that may not improve the final result.

The right value needs to be evaluated against both retrieval quality and latency.

I also addressed a different problem: finding the nearest result doesn't mean finding sufficient evidence.

A retrieval system will often return something, even when the query isn't adequately supported by the available documents.

Passing that weak evidence directly to an LLM can lead to unsupported answers.

To reduce this risk, I added a similarity cutoff and a "no relevant context" fallback.

However, a threshold isn't a guarantee of relevance.

A permissive threshold can admit weak evidence. A strict threshold can reject useful chunks.

The threshold needs to be calibrated against evaluation data rather than chosen arbitrarily.

I then defined a retrieval contract so downstream components can consume results without depending on the internal implementation of vector search, BM25, RRF, or reranking.

I also wrote unit tests that verify known source chunks appear in the top three results for their associated questions.

These tests give me a repeatable way to catch ranking regressions.

But they don't prove that retrieval performs well across the entire document collection. That requires a broader evaluation set with representative queries and relevance judgments.

I'm also treating failure handling as part of the retrieval design.

What happens if:

→ The BM25 index becomes stale?
→ One retrieval method returns malformed results?
→ The cross-encoder times out?
→ No candidate meets the relevance threshold?

Each case needs an explicit failure policy. Otherwise, a problem in one stage can silently degrade the quality of the complete pipeline.

The biggest lesson from Day 135:

Advanced RAG isn't about adding more retrieval techniques. It's about understanding how ranking quality, computational cost, and failure handling interact across the pipeline.
I now have:
→ Hybrid vector and BM25 retrieval
→ Reciprocal Rank Fusion
→ Cross-encoder reranking
→ A relevance cutoff and fallback
→ A defined retrieval contract
→ Known-chunk ranking tests
→ Explicit retrieval failure boundaries
The next step is to connect retrieval to answer generation.

DocMind needs to assemble retrieved chunks into context, generate answers grounded in that evidence, and produce reliable citations.

Then I'll evaluate whether these ranking decisions actually improve retrieval quality, answer correctness, and end-to-end latency.

Day 135 wasn't just about combining search methods.

It was about building a retrieval layer that knows not only what to return, but also when the available evidence isn't good enough.

We are nowhere near the top. The AI bubble is just beginning. 

Three technical trends explain why:

Scaling laws are expanding. Performance gains now come from pretraining compute, reinforcement learning, and test-time compute. The compute required per complex task can increase even as token costs decline.

Inference is becoming the dominant workload. Agentic systems execute multi-step workflows with recursive tool calls, long context windows, and repeated model invocations. A single task can require orders of magnitude more tokens than a chatbot query.

Compute efficiency is driving demand elasticity. Improvements in FLOP/$ and tokens/joule lower the cost of intelligence. If workload growth exceeds efficiency gains, aggregate compute demand continues to increase.

And we haven’t fully deployed persistent agents, multimodal world models, or real-time embodied AI.

The critical variable isn’t the price per token… that’s irrelevant… what really matters is total compute consumed per unit of economic output.

We may be underestimating the compute intensity of the next generation of AI applications.

The best is yet to come.

The guy who invented Amazon Prime disappeared for six years. He came back this week with $250 million and a factory that turns lines of code into tiny working machines. Type different code, a different machine comes out the other end.

That sounds fake. Here's why it took six years.

A chip fab is the most precise factory humans have ever built, and it makes exactly one kind of thing. Flat silicon that processes information. The moment you want moving parts, multiple materials, or real 3D structure, you leave the fab for a world where getting one new device into production takes years and tens of millions of dollars. Engineers call it one product, one process. It's the reason micro-machines never got their Moore's Law.

Holden's Matter Compiler kills the per-product process entirely. Features down to a few microns, no new tooling, and the system measures and corrects every step while it builds, then feeds what it learned into the next design.

His first product is the tell on how sharp the strategy is.

PrimeSwitch is a 150-amp relay for 800-volt power in AI data centers. It opens in roughly 50 microseconds, about 1,000x faster than a normal contactor. So the first thing to come out of a universal factory is aimed at the one market where demand is basically infinite and a faster switch means less fried hardware.

Neal Stephenson wrote the Matter Compiler as fiction in 1995. Holden just shipped the first real product out of one, and it's a light switch for AI data centers.

Around 3 weeks ago introduced Laya, the first open-source version of JEV, and it has reached a very large scale. Today I am open-sourcing a new physics-based typed decision model called Vega.
The interesting parts. It is only 800 million parameters (4B is also there), with 73k token support, image support, and surpassing many of the jev benchmarks in single-shot. Implemented an engine+adapter as a Test-Time Training Architecture.
Imagine you are giving input to the model like "ignore all previous conversations," which is called the observation, along with a question, "Is this trying to override the instructions of the model?" and your possible outcomes are YES or NO. The whole prompt is passed to an LLM/VLM (yeah, image-supported), then from the hidden layers, we can extract the observation, question, the yes and no, and last token. These will be vectors, and we can project it by multiplying with wieghts; then, first, using the observation projection, we can create a landscape with valleys; then, using the question and last-token vectors, we can initialise a ball in the valley, and using YES or NO, we can get the candidate location of the ball. Depends on the number of outcomes we create valleys; that is, here YES and NO, so 2. When the ball fall on YES valley, we get the answer. There is friction also influencing how the ball moves.
TLDR: It's like creating valleys of outcomes that we need and throwing a ball that will slow down based on friction and settle on the best outcome

How fast should your UI animate?

I built a motion system for Superstocks. It could be duplicated for any other product or website.

One rule first: every action needs a feedback. Keyword here: feedback. Not necesserarily an animation.

Then two families.

1. Feedback
For UI elements that are used often. It starts immediately and settles quickly. Default is 175ms, with a snappy easing.

2. Presence
For new elements that weren't part of the interface, or aren't an extension of something inside it: a modal, a drawer. Slow in, fast out. Default is 275ms.

Both families share the same 8 presets: default, slow, fast, snap, bounce, elastic, accelerate, decelerate. Same names, different timings and easing.

Most of the easings come from https://t.co/KuBTCzwRM0, some are tweaked a bit, so animations are never boring and linear.

Used all the time? Keep it speedy.
New on screen? Animate its presence: snap is 300ms on a control, 475ms on an element entering the view.

I tested it a lot then documented it for my coding agent so whenever implementing something new, it instantly feels part of the system.

Software architecture is pointless if it's easy to break.

Here's how you fix this.

I use 3 approaches to enforce architecture:

- Compiler, static analysis
- Architecture testing
- Code reviews (with AI)

The compiler is your best friend. It won't let you make a mistake. If you write code that doesn't compile, your builds crash. Instant feedback.

How does this help you enforce software architecture?

In .NET you can:

- Use the internal access modifier to hide types from other assemblies
- Organize your code into separate projects (assemblies) to enforce isolation

But that doesn't scale well because you end up with too many projects.

Static analysis is powerful. But I don't like writing custom Roslyn rules. Although you could try this out with AI. I reckon it will do a pretty good job at it.

I prefer architecture testing. Architecture tests let me express my design rules as automated tests. I can use them to enforce the correct design.

For example, in a modular monolith, each module can only reference the public API of other modules.

Here's how architecture testing can help you "shift left": https://t.co/0kKfBjXxTp

Lastly, code reviews. This should be self-explanatory. Someone has to review the code and approve it manually. But with AI-generated PRs this is not a good use of your time. I'd use manual review with AI as a helper to speed this up.

Most developers have good intentions. Time pressure, misunderstandings, and resistance to rules can turn a codebase into slop.

Even the most well-planned software projects decay because of technical debt.

Architecture testing acts as a safeguard.

🤯 What if your AI coding agent could learn from every real coding session… and build its own skill library?

Not by manually adding prompts.

Not by stacking hundreds of random instructions.

By learning from the work it already does.

That's AutoHarness — a self-learning skill layer for Claude Code.

Here's what makes it interesting:

→ Learns from real work: Turns useful lessons from coding sessions into reusable skills in the background.

→ Improves existing skills: When a new lesson corrects an old one, it can update the existing skill instead of creating another.

→ Merges duplicates: Similar skills get consolidated into a cleaner, more useful library.

→ Tracks what actually gets used: Skills can be evaluated based on whether the agent loads them when relevant work comes up.

→ Retires outdated skills: Unused skills can be archived, with their history preserved.

And there's one detail I really like.

It only manages the skills it created itself.

Your manually written skills and skills installed from elsewhere are left untouched.

Every change also gets a ledger containing the reason and supporting evidence.

The bigger idea?

Today's AI agents rely on humans to maintain their prompts, instructions and workflows.

AutoHarness explores a different approach:

Let the agent learn reusable workflows from experience — then maintain that knowledge as it evolves.

The model stays the same. The harness gets better.

How to turn an LLM into a decision model?

Say we have a support ticket that says, “I was charged twice for invoice 4411. Please refund.”

Our application needs to make two decisions. Which team should handle the ticket, and whether to issue a refund.

An LM would generate text token by token while a decision model would score the available choices directly.

Here’s how to turn an LLM into one:

→ Define the questions and choices.

Give the model the ticket alongside the decisions to make. For the team, the choices are billing, technical, and sales. For the refund, they are yes and no.

→ Keep the backbone and freeze its weights.

The backbone processes the input and builds internal representations of it. Add LoRA, small trainable components that adapt those representations while the original weights stay frozen.

→ Replace the language model head.

The language model head predicts the next token. Replace it with a decision head that gathers evidence from the ticket for each option, lets the questions and options interact, and produces one score per choice.

→ Convert scores into probabilities.

Apply softmax, which converts scores into probabilities, separately for each question. You get one probability distribution over the teams and another over the refund choices.

→ Train on the correct answers.

For this training example, the labels are billing and yes. Cross-entropy loss measures how well the predictions match those labels, and training updates only the decision head and LoRA components.

→ Calibrate on held-out examples.

After training, use examples excluded from training to adjust the model’s confidence. Its predicted probabilities should reflect how often those predictions are correct.

At inference time, one forward pass scores all the choices. Your application gets probabilities it can use to route the ticket and make the refund decision.

I trained a JEV-style decision model locally using Qwen3.5 0.8B. Accuracy went from 37% to 65% in just 60 steps, with 10 minutes of training on 4GB of VRAM.

Check out my YouTube video for the full walkthrough, from setup and training to evaluation and inference.

Possibilties of models like Astra are really impressive. While exploring my early version of the labyrinth skill (on GitHub) I have tested it against a nasty problem from algebra. Philips and Stanovský have proved in 2012 that Bruck loops with abelian inner mapping groups are centrally nilpotent of class at most 2.

Their proof contains a standard paper argument and an extremely long certificate produced by Waldmeister, a high performance equation theorem prover. Their certifacte has about 1000 pages. In the paper the authors formulated Problem 5: Find a "human friendly" proof of Theorem 1.

Autocompaction is effectively Artificial Alzheimer, and it may work in your agent's favor or against it.

The way it works is simple. It runs a prompt like "summarize this conversation and keep only what's essential" at a specific context utilization threshold and then injects the response into a compacted context.

Forgetting irrelevant context helps, but it can also drop important context or nuance, so after autocompaction you're dealing with an AI agent who has just suffered memory loss while trying to continue work from looking at some fragmented notes.

You can customize the compaction prompt and add instructions about what summaries must retain, but it won't solve the fundamental issue that this is a lossy operation.

What I've seen working well is to ask the agent to persist important information about the current work in a scratchpad stored in a persistent file outside the conversation context, which survives compaction.

After compaction, the agent can then reread it and recover important things like decisions, requirements, progress, issues, next steps, etc.

To make this work though, you must make sure the agent discovers and reads it post compaction.

One way to do that is to write an explicit instruction in your project's CLAUDE.md, like:

> Read tmp/scratchpad.md at the start of every session and after context compaction. Treat it as the source of truth for current progress, decisions, and next steps.

But this is not reliable because the agent might not recognize the compaction as such or might simply miss applying the rule. Also, you will want to have one scratchpad per session!

So a more reliable approach is to use a deterministic `SessionStart` hook with the `compact|resume` matcher, which fires automatically after compaction or session resumption.

This can be done in .claude/settings.json, like this:

```
{
  "hooks": {
    "SessionStart": [
      {
        "matcher": "compact|resume",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "ID=$(jq -r '.session_id') && FILE=\"$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR/tmp/scratchpad-$ID.md\" && if [ -f \"$FILE\" ]; then cat \"$FILE\"; fi"
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

Note this requires jq, a lightweight command-line tool for reading and processing JSON. You might have to run `brew install jq` on macOS.

Your CLAUDE.md then needs an instruction to maintain the scratchpad. I'll post that in the comments.

Important: The scratchpad must be updated or else your agent gets confused by stale information.

Keep in mind, even with that, compaction means the agent has forgotten something. So compacting early may save you some tokens, but it might also mean your agent just forgot something important.

Hope this helps!

JEPA is one of the best ideas in how machines can learn about the world, however, it is still under-explored which parts of the state it learns stay the same and which parts change.

For example, a coffee mug looks different in bright morning sunlight and in dim light at night, but my hand still reaches for the same spot, because my brain keeps where the mug is separate from the lighting, which changes but does not matter for reaching.

Our new paper, SplitJEPA, gives JEPA this same separation in the state it learns.

In fact, the LeJEPA line of work from @ylecun, @randall_balestr, and @klindt_david already proves something strong here. Under stationary Gaussian predictive dynamics, they show that latent prediction with Gaussian regularization recovers the complete latent state up to a global orthogonal transformation, with no reconstruction needed at all.

That remaining transformation is where our paper begins.

Picture a map where every distance between cities is correct but there is no compass. Technically, nothing is missing, yet you still cannot tell which way is north. 

For LeJEPA, any orthogonal transformation of the learned state is an equally optimal solution, so each dimension of the learned representation can be a linear combination of invariant factors, which are shared across related observations, and variant factors, which change between them.

SplitJEPA adds that compass. It divides the representation into an invariant block and a variant block, and alongside the predictive pairs it also trains on invariant pairs, where the two observations in a pair share the invariant factors and differ in the variant factors, such as the same physical state rendered from two cameras.

An agreement loss requires the invariant block to match across each pair, which removes its linear dependence on the variant factors. Because the full transformation is orthogonal, once the invariant block holds exactly the invariant factors, the variant block is left with exactly the variant factors.

The key condition is sufficient variation. SplitJEPA requires the second-moment matrix of the variant changes across pairs to be full rank, meaning no variant factor, and no combination of them, remains unchanged across all pairs. A single pair does not need to change every factor though, since the condition is on the aggregate coverage.

We prove that under these conditions the invariant and variant subspaces are identified up to independent block-wise isometries, without introducing an observation decoder. 

The result is also stable. When the agreement holds only approximately, the leakage of variant factors into the invariant block is bounded in terms of the consistency error and the smallest eigenvalue of the variation matrix.

We evaluate SplitJEPA on PushCube, a ManiSkill simulation task where a robot arm must push a cube into a goal region on a table.

When the test camera is rotated 10 degrees around the scene (a camera pose not seen in training), behavior-cloning policies succeed only 12.8% of the time on raw pixels, and 48.0% on frozen R3M (a pre-trained visual representation for robot manipulation), while SplitJEPA achieves a 71.5% success rate.

LeJEPA showed that the latent state can be recovered without reconstruction, and SplitJEPA extends this to show that its invariant-variant organization can, and should, be recovered the same way.

What happens when a coding agent starts improving its own harness?

MIT and Sakana AI have been working on this with SIFT.

The idea is to let an agent propose changes to its own system, then test whether those changes actually help.

That sounds simple until you consider the cost.

Every candidate might need a full benchmark run.

If you test hundreds of changes, evaluation can cost more than the improvements are worth.

SIFT uses a different approach.

It lets an LLM judge compare candidate changes before running expensive evaluations.

The search can also explore new branches while earlier candidates are still running.

I think this is an interesting direction for harness engineering.

Imagine measuring changes to:

• Tool descriptions
• Context selection
• Compaction rules
• Agent instructions
• Planning behavior
• Recovery strategies

Then keeping only changes that improve performance on tasks the system hasn't seen before.

The hard part is preventing the harness from overfitting to the benchmark.

A change that improves SWE-bench might make the agent worse at real development tasks.

I would want to measure verified success, cost, regressions, and recovery across different projects before accepting an improvement.

Claude Code tip: if a subagent has to wait on tests or builds partway through, give it 𝗶𝘁𝘀 𝗼𝘄𝗻 𝟭-𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗰𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗲.

By default, a subagent's cache expires after 5 minutes with no activity. If it runs a test suite or waits on a build and sits idle for more than 5 minutes, its next step has to reprocess the whole context from scratch. That's slower than reading from the cache and counts more against your usage limits.

But 𝗱𝗼𝗻'𝘁 𝘀𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗰𝗵 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝘀𝘂𝗯𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝟭 𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗿. The official docs say 1-hour cache writes cost more (at API prices, 2x the base input price; 5-minute writes are 1.25x). Subagents that work straight through without pausing get nothing from the longer cache and just cost more.

Set it by job:
→ Subagents that sit idle for more than 5 minutes partway through, or that you'll resume later: add two lines at the top of the subagent's file, experimental: with cacheTtl: 1h indented under it
→ Ones that run straight through and finish in a few minutes: keep the default 5 minutes
→ If you already added subagentPromptCacheTtl to your settings: it 𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗿𝗶𝗱𝗲𝘀 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝘀𝘂𝗯𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁'𝘀 𝗼𝘄𝗻 𝘀𝗲𝘁𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 (I tested it), and it changes workflows and compaction too. To set them one by one, delete it first
→ On an API key, a cloud provider, or a subscription that's past its limit and drawing on usage credits: the main session only gets 5 minutes too. If you often step away mid-session, set promptCacheTtl to 1h
→ On a 1M-context model like Opus 5.5: by default it doesn't compact until about 967K tokens, and until then every message carries the whole conversation. Run /autocompact 400k once and it compacts at 400K

Send this prompt and the docs link below to Opus 5.5 in Claude Code 👇

"Read this doc, plus the subagent docs it links to, and set up my cache lifetimes by job:
1. First run claude --version. Setting cacheTtl on a single subagent needs 2.1.248 or later. If mine is older, tell me. Don't upgrade it yourself.
2. List every subagent in ~/.claude/agents and .claude/agents. For ones that might sit idle for more than 5 minutes partway through (running tests, builds, waiting on CI), or that I'll resume later, add these two lines at the top of the file:
experimental:
  cacheTtl: 1h
If there's already an experimental block, add cacheTtl under it. Don't write a second one. Leave the ones that run straight through and finish in a few minutes on the default. Give one line of reasoning for each.
3. Check ~/.claude/settings.json, .claude/settings.json and .claude/settings.local.json (including their env blocks) and my current environment variables for subagentPromptCacheTtl, CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_PROMPT_CACHE_TTL or FORCE_PROMPT_CACHING_5M. If any of them is set, tell me it overrides the per-subagent settings and ask whether to remove it.
4. Ask me whether I'm on a subscription, an API key or a cloud provider. Don't read any keys yourself. Unless I'm on a subscription within its plan usage, ask whether I often step away for more than 5 minutes mid-session, and if I do, set promptCacheTtl to 1h.
Show me what you'll change first, and don't write anything until I confirm."

A model picks the right answer — but says it is 99% sure when it is actually only 60% right. In a medical setting, that overconfidence on a wrong answer can shape a human's next decision. The problem is not just getting the answer right; it is making the model's stated confidence match its true accuracy.

National University of Singapore presents ConfTuner, accepted at NeurIPS 2025.

ConfTuner shares the core intuition behind the viral Jev model: output decision plus probability directly, support parallel probability prediction, treat probability as the core of prediction rather than an afterthought, and pursue probability calibration — not just choosing correctly, but making the stated probability reflect the true correctness rate. Where Jev is closed-source, ConfTuner is open and proposes the Tokenized Brier Score: a method that directly trains the probability distribution over candidate confidences, so the model's expressed "certainty" gets closer to its actual accuracy. The paper uses medical scenarios to illustrate how overconfidence on wrong answers can mislead downstream human judgment. Code and an extension project (JevTuner) are released.

Result: ConfTuner brings probability calibration to the core of prediction with Tokenized Brier Score — training candidate confidence distributions so stated certainty matches true accuracy — anticipating Jev's decision-plus-probability paradigm at NeurIPS 2025, with open code and JevTuner extension.

Top 10 API design mistakes I keep seeing:

1) No versioning plan. Shipping /v1 forever, then doing breaking changes behind the same route.
2) No idempotency for writes. Retries create duplicate orders, charges, tickets.
3) Ambiguous error model. Random 200 with error fields, no stable codes, no retry guidance.
4) Leaking internals. Exposing DB IDs, table-ish naming, or stack traces that become contracts.
5) Chatty endpoints. Mobile makes 12 calls to render one screen because you designed per-table APIs.
6) Missing pagination + filtering standards. No cursor, no max limits, no consistent sort order.
7) Weak auth boundaries. AuthN but no AuthZ, no scopes, no tenant isolation tests.
8) No timeouts or backpressure. Clients can hold connections forever, servers melt under slowloris.
9) Bad consistency semantics. Read-after-write assumptions with caches/replicas and no docs.
10) No observability hooks. No request IDs, no structured logs, no per-route latency/error metrics

Some thoughts on building a software factory on an M5U 256.

If you want to run a software factory on DeepSeek Flash, you'll spend at minimum $1000/mo, or possibly $500 if you're not running 24/7. That is assuming multiple threads with multiple subagents.

That means that after a year you've made back the cost of the system in API savings. 

So after you make the purchase you're incentivized to set up a workflow that can run mostly unattended with only occasional steering. 

That means you need to build up a long-term roadmap and a way for agents to build against the roadmap with less direct instruction.

That in turn means you need multiple agents because Flash models cannot be trusted to do proper planning and reviewing - they always need at least one audit layer by another agent because they're too tunnel visioned, miss details and make up information to fill those holes.

To replace DeepSeek Flash on a 256GB system the best  candidate right now is probably Qwen 3.8 Flash. Hopefully Qwen 4 Flash won't be too large.

With 3.8 Flash the highest decode we can expect is 200 tks. That means we probably do not want concurrency higher than 4. 

While we shift the rote tasks to local models, we'll need systems for CI, testing and more, which grows the TAM of those markets.

At the same time, we'll need to scale up frontier model usage for planning and reviewing as we generate more local tokens. 

So, if you buy an M5U 256, you take on the work of building an entirely new software development workflow, spending on the third party services that enable that workflow, and frontier models to keep the system and local agents running.

So, you cut token spend on some existing work, then you increase spend on work that didn't exist before you built the new system.

parent_text:
An LLM does not generate a sentence.
 
It generates one token.
Then another.
Then another.
 
But a lot happens before each token reaches your screen.
 
Here is the simplified inference pipeline:
 
Your prompt is split into tokens.
Each token is converted into a numerical embedding.
Transformer layers use attention and feed-forward networks to process the context.
The model produces a probability distribution across its vocabulary.
A decoding strategy selects the next token.
That token is added to the context, and the cycle repeats.
Tokens are converted back into text and streamed to you.
 
The most interesting part is that inference has two very different phases:
 
Prefill processes the input tokens largely in parallel.
 
Decode generates tokens sequentially, making memory movement, KV-cache size, and bandwidth increasingly important.
 
This is why:
 
 → Longer prompts increase prefill work
 → Longer conversations grow the KV cache
 → Quantization can reduce memory requirements
 → FlashAttention reduces expensive memory reads
 → Speculative decoding can improve generation speed
 → Temperature, Top-K, and Top-P change how the next token is selected
 
The model may look like it is "writing."
 
Underneath, it is repeatedly performing numerical operations, selecting a token, updating its context, and doing it all again.
 
I mapped the complete flow in one diagram.
 
Save it if you are learning how LLM inference actually works.

New JetBrains Research paper argues that coding-agent benchmarks should copy how their real users actually work, because real sessions mix and switch task types across many messages.

 Real developers using coding agents ask questions, plan, review, and switch tasks mid-session, but benchmarks like SWE-Bench Pro hand the agent 1 detailed issue and grade 1 final patch. In that benchmark, new features and bug fixes make up 93.8% of tasks.

JetBrains researchers studied 4,782 real agent sessions, where features and bug fixes were well under half of requests. In longer sessions, users kept switching between questions, planning, reviews, and edits.

They built SWE-TaskFlow, which splits each benchmark issue into several turns and adds checkable questions about the code. On 700 SWE-Bench Pro tasks, splitting roughly doubled agent cost with no stable change in success rate.

If you evaluate coding agents, first measure what your own users ask for, then shape the benchmark's conversation to match it.

– arxiv. org/abs/2610.09633

Title: "Coding-Agent Benchmarks Should Match Their Users' Task Flows"

AI agents can improve at new tasks by rewriting the code that runs them, while their model weights stay frozen!

A new paper explores "harness learning": training a model to revise another agent's harness, the code controlling its model calls, tools and information flow. It reads execution feedback, changes the workflow, and tries again. Once trained, it can do this on new tasks without further weight updates.

Across 21 unseen reasoning task families, average scores from revised harnesses rose from 32% with the untrained revision model to 62% after reinforcement learning. The trained 4B model even produced better revisions on average than its 35B teacher. In multi-hop question answering, improvements continued over repeated revision rounds and transferred to unseen benchmarks.

What I find exciting is that the ability to improve the workflow itself transfers. Imagine coding agents that learn from failed runs and adapt how they search, test and use tools. This paper gives us a concrete reason to pursue that.

Most AI code review platforms have a hidden problem:

They waste money reviewing code that has already changed.

Imagine a developer pushes 5 commits in 60 seconds.

Do you run 5 separate AI reviews?

That means 5 expensive inference jobs, duplicate findings, wasted tokens, and feedback on code that may no longer exist.

Checkout this how you can design this:

1. Debounce review requests

- When a commit arrives, push a review job into a queue.

- Wait for a short window, say 10-15 seconds.

- If more commits arrive for the same PR, keep updating the pending job instead of starting a new review immediately.

2. Review the latest snapshot

- Once the window closes, fetch the latest PR state.

- Review the combined diff against the target branch, not every intermediate commit.

- Five commits can now trigger one review instead of five.

3. Deduplicate expensive work

- Generate a fingerprint using the changed file, diff content, model version, and review configuration.

- If the exact same analysis already exists, reuse its result.

- Use an idempotency key so duplicate queue deliveries don't start duplicate jobs.

4. Don't make developers wait

Run fast, deterministic checks first:

- Linting
- Type checking
- Static analysis

Then stream AI findings as they become available.

Developers get quick feedback while deeper analysis continues in the background.

5. Cancel stale reviews

- Suppose a review is already running when another commit arrives.

- Mark the old review as stale.

- Cancel it if possible. 

Otherwise, let it finish, but don't publish outdated findings as the latest review.

6. Control inference costs

- Use a cheap model for routine checks and a stronger model for complex changes.

- Analyze only relevant code, pull in surrounding context when needed, and cache reusable results.

The architecture:

Git webhook → Review coordinator → Debounce + deduplication → Queue → Static checks → AI workers → Results store → Live updates

One important detail: every review must be tied to a specific commit SHA.

Otherwise, results from an older snapshot can overwrite newer feedback.

The key principle:

Don't review every event.

Review the latest meaningful state.

That's how you reduce AI costs without sacrificing developer experience.

Decision models deliver structured answers or classifications with associated probabilities, offering faster responses and lower costs than using language models. The Artificial Analysis Decision Index v1.0 compares the capability, cost, and speed of decision models and also compares to language models.

Benchmarks in the Artificial Analysis Decision Index v1.0:

➤ AA-Omniscience-Decision: A private dataset of 500 questions adapted from the proprietary AA-Omniscience benchmark, measuring decision models’ knowledge and tendency to hallucinate

➤ HLE-MultiChoice: 513 text-only multiple-choice questions from Humanity’s Last Exam, testing decision models’ reasoning capabilities

➤ When2Call: A tool-calling benchmark from NVIDIA, testing whether models can correctly decide to call a tool, request clarification, decline to answer, or respond directly, evaluating capabilities relevant to agentic workflows and tool routing

➤ WildGuardTest: A safety benchmark evaluating models’ classification capabilities across harmful user requests, assistant refusals, and harmful responses. We use a subset of 835 of the original 1,725 test rows where all three human annotators agreed on all three labels, after excluding questions that consistently trigger model refusals

Key results:

➤ Jev 1.13 leads the Decision Index, and sits on the Capability vs. Cost Pareto frontier: Jev 1.13 from @typesafeai scores 58 on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index, ahead of GLiDE (54) from @fastinoAI and Microsoft-Decision-1 (54) from @Microsoft. Decider v1.1 27B from @perplexity_ai has the lowest Cost per 1M Tasks at $17, with Microsoft-Decision-1 ($31) and Jev 1.13 ($42) also on the Capability vs. Cost Pareto frontier. Celeris-1 Decision has the fastest Time per Task at 0.06 seconds, more than 2x faster than Jev 1.13 (0.13 seconds per task)

➤ Decision models are poorly calibrated on knowledge and reasoning tasks: Across almost all probability levels for chosen answers, accuracy falls below that probability for all decision models. This gap is largest on AA-Omniscience-Decision and HLE-MultiChoice, while most models are relatively well-calibrated on WildGuardTest (classification) and When2Call (tool calling)

➤ Decision models offer significant speed and cost advantages over language models, but trail on knowledge and reasoning: On classification and tool-calling tasks, leading decision models perform comparably to language models while being significantly faster and cheaper. However, language models substantially outperform on knowledge and reasoning. Claude Haiku 5.5 (Low) scores 61 on the Decision Index, 3 points ahead of Jev 1.13, but takes 1.4 seconds per task vs. 0.13 seconds (11x slower) and costs $184 per 1M Tasks vs. $42 for Jev 1.13 (4.4x more expensive)

We will continue to develop the Artificial Analysis Decision Index to help developers and companies better understand when and how to use decision models.

Cache hit rates and Cost per Task by provider are now live on Artificial Analysis: Cost per Task for GLM-5.3 (max) varies ~9x across providers, driven by a combination of cache hit rate and token pricing

Agentic workloads resend the full conversation history every turn, so most input tokens are cacheable, and cache pricing and cache hit rates drive most of the gap in Cost per Task. We already use measured cache hit rates to calculate Cost per Task, and are now publishing them for each model endpoint we track.

What's new:
➤ Cache hit rates are now visible for all first-party and third-party endpoints, measured by running multi-turn agentic coding tasks and reading cached tokens from each provider's usage response. Cache hit rate is the share of cacheable input tokens served from cache.
➤ Cost per Task is now available by provider for open weights models, calculated from each provider's input, output, cache hit and cache write prices, applied at its measured cache hit rate. To standardize across providers for a given model, we use the same input, output and cacheable token counts from the model's Intelligence Index run.

Key takeaways:
➤ Cost per Task on GLM-5.3 (max) spans ~9x across providers, from $0.92 on Makora to $8.68 on Nebius. Both serve nearly all cacheable input from cache (98% and 100%) and charge the same output price ($4.40 per 1M tokens), so the gap comes from input pricing: Makora charges $0.10 per 1M cached input tokens, while Nebius offers no cached input discount on its shared serverless endpoints and bills all input at the full $1.40.
➤ Cache hit rate ranges from 41% to 100% across 21 providers (25 endpoints). 15 endpoints are at 98% or above, and eight are at 100%: Modal, DeepInfra, Parasail, Together AI, DigitalOcean, Nebius, Novita and Z AI's first-party API. Multiverse Computing is lowest at 41%, followed by Bitdeer at 50%.
